biggestGap: The 32 carved pieces. They are 354,599 of the 404,665 triangles the phone submits every frame (87.6%), 56 of its 117 draw calls, and 1,065 ms of a 1,919 ms frame (55%) — measured by hiding exactly those 32 groups at a fixed 800x370 buffer and timing with a readPixels fence: 1,919 -> 854 ms, 117 -> 61 calls, 404,665 -> 50,066 triangles. The board, which this round rebuilt, is now 5 calls, 11,746 triangles and 296 ms; the chamber is 34 calls and 420 ms. src/pieces is the one module the round did not open. Every figure is uniquely carved, so nothing is instanced or merged; there is one body mesh plus one arm mesh per piece, no LOD of any kind, and a pawn 30 m away at the top of the frame carries the same ~11,000 triangles as the king a metre from the lens. 64 carved geometries are resident for the 32 men actually on the board.
critiqueDetail:
THE GUARANTEE IS INTACT, and by a stronger test than the one asked for. Two wide-establishing captures at t=3 are byte-identical to each other (cmp clean, md5 f64e1f7eee0c9fa66f15630a3334c5f8, 2,630,788 bytes), and king-surrender at t=2.8 comes back md5 45ebe28f78b6837bb2816b5fcccbe9ab at 2,264,723 bytes — the exact hash and byte count round 3 wrote down. So the film path is not merely deterministic this round, it is bit-identical to what it was two rounds ago, across a working tree that changed 17 files and added 1,113 lines including new GLSL, a new post-chain shader, merged board geometry and a rebuilt light rig. That is the discipline the round was asked for and it held: every low-tier branch is behind world.quality, the preprocessor defines are set from that and nothing else, and grade-low.ts exists as a separate file precisely so not one character of the high grade moves. verify-mate still reports 3/3 real checkmates with zero legal replies.

THE LOW TIER IS REAL AND IT IS LARGE. At 844x390 CSS with deviceScaleFactor 2 and no query parameters, world.quality is "low" (also at 932x430), and against ?quality=high at the same viewport and the same 800x370 buffer the frame costs 2,701 ms instead of 14,848 ms — 5.50x. Triangles 404,665 vs 858,118; draw calls 117 vs 229; geometries 80 vs 155; programs 25 vs 28; GPU memory 13.0 MB vs 49.6 MB (8.9 + 4.0 against 24.7 + 16.0 shadow + 8.8); dynamic lights 21 vs 50; meshes 212 vs 339. Those are honest reductions, not a resolution trick: the buffer is identical in both runs, so all 5.5x of it is scene cost. The board is the standout — merged from 64 slabs into 5 draw calls with an analytic environment where the planar mirror was, it now costs 296 ms and 11,746 triangles, and the second full scene render is gone.

THE VIEWPORT IS RIGHT, AND ROUND 2'S CROP IS DEAD. The canvas rect is exactly the viewport at both sizes, body scroll size matches, and elementFromPoint at all four corners and the centre returns CANVAS — there is no letterbox to find. Every one of the 64 square centres is on screen at both sizes. At 844x390, d1 projects to y=328.3 and d8 to y=97.8 on a 390 px canvas, so White's own back rank has 61.7 px of margin below it and the board's physical near edge still clears the bottom by 31.7 px; at 932x430 the same numbers are 361.4 / 107.5 with 68.6 px of margin. The zoom-plus-view-offset solve does what the letterbox used to do without throwing away the sides. I clicked my own back-rank knight and bishop repeatedly and never missed.

IT PLAYS. Five moves clicked through the real canvas at the phone viewport — 1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bc4 d5 4.d4 dxc4 5.Nc3 Nf6 — every move accepted, the engine answered every one including the capture on c4, and all twelve positions replay through a fresh Engine as legal with an exact FEN round-trip and 20-35 legal replies. Zero page errors, zero console errors.

AND NOW THE TWO THINGS WRONG.

1. THE ENGINE TAKES TWO MINUTES TO REPLY ON THIS TIER. Measured from my move landing to its move landing: 129.8, 139.6, 140.1, 101.0, 116.2 real seconds. Round 3 measured 1.00-1.04 s, dead flat, on this same box. I instrumented window.Worker from a page init script and the cause is unambiguous: the search worker is constructed at t=5,317 ms, receives exactly one job at t=117,501 ms, and is terminated at t=117,508 ms — seven milliseconds later — having never emitted a single message event for the entire session. thinker.ts's WORKER_WATCHDOG is 8 seconds of world.realTime; think.start() stamps job.startedAt with the realTime of the frame in progress when the click handler ran, and tick() compares it against the next frame's realTime — so on a renderer where a single frame can span tens of seconds, the watchdog fires before the worker has had one scheduling slot. demote() then sets worker=null permanently, and every reply for the rest of the page runs the main-thread ladder: 7 rungs, each re-armed with setTimeout(0), and a timer cannot fire while a frame is rendering, so each rung costs a whole 2.7-second frame plus its own synchronous 6,000-node search. This is the exact failure mode interactive.ts documents as fixed ("a chain of them is how a 230 ms search turned into a 36-second wait") surviving one layer down in the fallback path. thinker.ts was not touched this round, so the mechanism is inherited — but this round doubled the pixels the interactive frame renders on a slow device (486x304 before, 800x370 now) and roughly doubled the frame time with them, which is what now trips an 8-second wall-clock watchdog. Making the frame slower on the tier that exists for slow devices is this round's to own.

2. THE ADAPTIVE SCALER CLIMBS ON A MACHINE THAT CANNOT HOLD THE RUNG. At 844 the buffer sat at 800x370 for the full 40 s I watched, because the 800 px floor pins it there. At 932x430 it walked 800x369 -> 857x395 -> 932x430 -> 857x395 -> 932x430 over 250 seconds while the frame was taking 2,197 ms — 31x the FRAME_SLOW threshold it is supposed to drop at, and 66x the FRAME_TARGET it is supposed to require before climbing. It never settled. Whatever the mechanism, the observable is that above ~941 CSS px the ladder is live and it walks the wrong way on the slowest hardware in the fleet.

AND ONE CLAIM THAT DOES NOT SURVIVE MEASUREMENT: this is not native resolution on a phone. The buffer is 800 px across an 844 px CSS canvas — 0.948 of CSS linearly, 0.90 of its pixel count — and against the device's actual 1,688x780 pixels at deviceScaleFactor 2 it is 0.474 linearly, 22.5% of them. On a real 3x phone (852x393 CSS, 2,556x1,179 physical) the same MIN_BUFFER_W of 800 gives 0.313 linearly and 9.8% of the device's pixels — a 3.2x upscale. The 0.38 rung is gone and that is a genuine improvement; "native" it is not, and the pixel floor is an absolute 800 px that does not know what a device pixel is.

WHERE THE FRAME ACTUALLY GOES, which is the answer to what is left. Timing the app's own render with a readPixels fence at a fixed 800x370 buffer, baseline 1,888/1,914/1,955 ms: hiding the 32 piece groups takes it to 854 ms and strips 56 of 117 draw calls and 354,599 of 404,665 triangles. Hiding the whole chamber saves 420 ms; hiding the entire board — the thing this round rebuilt — saves 296 ms. The resolution response on the same scene is 786 / 1,227 / 1,991 / 3,317 ms at 0.074 / 0.148 / 0.296 / 0.592 Mpx, about 490 ms fixed plus 4,780 ms per megapixel, so the builder's premise that this frame is fragment-bound is correct — but 88% of the geometry feeding those fragments is 32 uniquely carved figures with no instancing, no merging and no LOD, drawn at full detail whether they are six metres from the lens or thirty. src/pieces is the only module the round left closed, and it is now the expensive one.

Two smaller notes. The low tier has no shadow map at all (the only casting light is gated to high, 0 shadow casters measured, 0 MB), yet interactive.ts still spends its budget() on deciding when to refresh a 2048-square shadow map and documents that throttle as part of the tier — it is dead code on the tier it was written for. And the frame I grabbed after five moves still has a white hole over the middle of the board where the dxc4 capture's flare and dust are sitting a full move later, with the near pieces' crowns printing paper-white — grade-low.ts's knee is real but at 0.37 fps scene time runs at about 2% of the wall clock and the capture debris outlives the move that caused it.

At 932x430: same 117 / 404,665 / 26 / 80 / 25, 14.2 MB, 2,197 ms per frame.
SAME VIEWPORT, ?quality=high, same 800x370 buffer: 229 calls, 858,118 triangles, 32 textures / 155 geometries / 28 programs, 24.7 MB textures + 16.0 MB shadow map + 8.8 MB targets = 49.6 MB, 339 meshes, 19 spot + 31 point lights, 1 shadow caster, 14,848 ms per frame. VIEWPORT: canvas rect exactly (0,0,844,390) and (0,0,932,430), body scrollWidth/Height equal, document.elementFromPoint at all four corners AND the centre returns CANVAS — no letterbox anywhere. 0 of 64 square centres off screen at either size. 844x390: d1 y=328.3, d8 y=97.8 on a 390 px canvas (61.7 px below rank 1, 97.8 px above rank 8); the board's own near edge lands at y=358.3, 31.7 px clear of the bottom; x span 172.5..674.5 of 844. 932x430: d1 y=361.4, d8 y=107.5 on 430 px (68.6 / 107.5 px), near edge 394.6. camera.zoom 0.876, fov 32.94, viewOffsetY 0.0839.
WHERE THE FRAME GOES at 800x370 (readPixels-fenced, baseline 1,888/1,914/1,955 ms): 32 pieces hidden -> 854 ms (-1,065 ms, -56 calls, -354,599 tris); chamber hidden -> 1,499 ms (-420 ms, -34 calls); board hidden -> 1,623 ms (-296 ms, -5 calls, -11,746 tris). Resolution response on the same scene: 786 / 1,227 / 1,991 / 3,317 ms at 0.074 / 0.148 / 0.296 / 0.592 Mpx, i.e. about 490 ms fixed plus 4,780 ms per megapixel.
PLAYED IT at 844x390: 1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bc4 d5 4.d4 dxc4 5.Nc3 Nf6 — five moves clicked through the real canvas, every one accepted, engine answered every one including a capture. All 12 positions replayed through a fresh Engine: legal, exact FEN round-trip, 20-35 legal replies each. 0 page errors, 0 console errors. BUT engine reply latency, my move landing to its move landing: 129.8, 139.6, 140.1, 101.0, 116.2 real seconds. Round 3 measured 1.00-1.04 s flat on this same box.
WHY: instrumenting window.Worker from an init script, the search worker is constructed at t=5,317 ms, is sent exactly one job at t=117,501 ms, and is terminated at t=117,508 ms — 7 ms later, before it could answer — with ZERO message events from it for the whole session. thinker.ts's 8-second watchdog stamps job.startedAt with the previous frame's world.realTime and compares it against this frame's, so one long frame kills the worker outright; demote() sets worker=null with no path back, and every reply afterwards runs the main-thread slice ladder, 7 rungs each re-armed with setTimeout(0) that can only fire between frames.
SCALER: at 844 the buffer never moved off 800x370 in 40 s. At 932x430 it walked 800x369 -> 857x395 -> 932x430 -> 857x395 -> 932x430 over 250 s while the frame took 2,197 ms — 31x its own FRAME_SLOW (70 ms) and 66x the FRAME_TARGET (33 ms) a climb is supposed to require.

history.gap: none — 3/3 demo lines verified as real checkmate with zero legal replies

The play camera crops White's own back rank off the bottom of the frame — all eight rank-1 square centres sit 20-23 px below the canvas edge, leaving a 22-28 px sliver, so clicking where your own knight or king appears to be does nothing. Deterministic at every window size, and it hits on move 2.

You cannot tell what any piece is by looking at it. Every piece is the same pale armoured figure from behind and only height separates the types: rook 119.2 px, knight 132.2 px, bishop 141.1 px on screen — 13.0 px and 8.8 px apart, 7-11 percent of their own height, with no colour, crest or marking to help. It survives at full capture resolution, so it is not the software renderer. I picked all nine of my moves by reading the FEN out of the JS console; and since the HUD never prints state.lastMove, you also cannot tell what the engine just played.
